topics.title: SQL Expression
topics.definition: A formula that combines columns, literal values, operators, or functions.
bullets: Produces a value that a query can use.
In a WHERE clause, a Boolean expression decides which rows qualify.
Expressions can be used when retrieving, updating, or deleting data.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: An expression, as you’ll recall, is a formula made up of

example.text:
SELECT creditLimit + 1000 AS adjustedLimit
FROM customers;

topics.title: SELECT — Retrieve Data
topics.definition: SELECT reads data from one or more tables.
bullets: The select list chooses the columns or expressions to show.
FROM names the source table.
Without WHERE, all source rows qualify.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The SELECT statement allows you to read data from one or more tables.

example.text:
SELECT lastName
FROM employees;

topics.title: Select List
topics.definition: The columns or expressions written after SELECT determine the output fields.
bullets: One name selects one column; commas separate multiple columns.
The output follows the order of the select list.
Selecting three columns does not change the other columns in the table.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
a list of 
columns or expressions that you want to show in the result.

example.text:
SELECT lastName, firstName, jobTitle
FROM employees;

topics.title: SQL Keyword Formatting
topics.definition: SQL keywords can be written in uppercase or lowercase.
bullets: SELECT and select have the same keyword meaning.
Line breaks and indentation improve readability; they are not required between clauses.
Database and table name case sensitivity can depend on settings and the operating system; MySQL/MariaDB column names are not case-sensitive.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: you can write the keywords in lowercase

corrections.text: The PDF says SQL is not case-sensitive. This is safe for keywords, but not a universal rule for identifiers or string comparisons.
corrections.label: MariaDB identifier case sensitivity

topics.title: Semicolon — Statement Delimiter
topics.definition: A semicolon marks the end of a statement in SQL clients and scripts.
bullets: Use it to separate multiple statements.
Place it after the final clause.
A single statement sent through an application API does not universally require it.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The semicolon ; is the statement delimiter.

example.text:
SELECT lastName FROM employees;
SELECT jobTitle FROM employees;

topics.title: Logical SELECT Evaluation
topics.definition: The source rows are established before the select list produces the displayed values.
bullets: For a basic query, think FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY.
This is a logical model; the database optimizer can choose a different physical execution plan.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
MySQL evaluates the FROM clause first and then the 
SELECT clause:

topics.title: Result Order Without ORDER BY
topics.definition: A query without ORDER BY has no guaranteed row order.
bullets: Rows can appear in any order.
Insertion order or a previous result is not a reliable sorting rule.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: the rows in the result set can be in any order.

topics.title: ORDER BY — Sort Results
topics.definition: ORDER BY sorts the rows returned by a query.
bullets: Write the sort columns or expressions after ORDER BY.
ASC means ascending; DESC means descending.
Each sort expression defaults to ASC when no direction is written.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
To sort the result set, you 
add the ORDER BY clause

topics.title: ASC and DESC
topics.definition: ASC sorts from lower to higher values; DESC sorts from higher to lower values.
bullets: Write the direction after the column it applies to.
Text ordering follows the column’s collation.
A direction on one column does not automatically apply to the next column.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The ASC stands for ascending and the DESC stands for descending.

topics.title: Sorting by Multiple Columns
topics.definition: Later sort columns break ties in earlier sort columns.
bullets: Separate sort expressions with commas.
ORDER BY lastName DESC, firstName ASC sorts last names descending, then first names ascending within equal last names.
The second sort does not reorder groups established by the first.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
only the order of values in the column2 
changes.

corrections.text: Page 72 says ORDER BY column1, column2 makes column2 descending. Both default to ascending; write DESC explicitly.
corrections.label: MariaDB ORDER BY

topics.title: WHERE — Filter Rows
topics.definition: WHERE keeps rows whose search condition evaluates to TRUE.
bullets: FALSE and UNKNOWN do not qualify.
Use WHERE in SELECT, UPDATE, or DELETE to choose affected rows.
In the logical SELECT sequence, WHERE follows FROM and precedes SELECT.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The WHERE clause allows you to specify a search condition

topics.title: Predicate and Search Condition
topics.definition: A predicate is a Boolean expression; a search condition combines predicates to filter rows.
bullets: Its result can be TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN.
AND, OR, and NOT combine or reverse conditions.
UNKNOWN commonly appears when a comparison involves NULL.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
a predicate is a Boolean expression that evaluates 
to TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN

topics.title: Equality Operator (=)
topics.definition: The equality operator tests whether two values are equal.
bullets: Use column = value to match a specific value.
Quote text literals, such as Sales Rep.
Use IS NULL rather than = NULL to test for missing values.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: whose value in the jobTitle column is Sales Rep.

topics.title: Combining Row Filters
topics.definition: AND and OR combine several row conditions into one search condition.
bullets: AND requires every condition to be true.
OR accepts either or both conditions being true.
Use parentheses when mixing them to make the intended grouping clear.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: AND operator evaluates to TRUE only if both expressions evaluate to TRUE.

topics.title: NOT — Reverse a Condition
topics.definition: NOT reverses a Boolean condition.
bullets: NOT TRUE is FALSE; NOT FALSE is TRUE.
NOT UNKNOWN remains UNKNOWN.
Parentheses make the condition being reversed clear.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
logical 
operator AND, OR and NOT.

topics.title: BETWEEN — Inclusive Range
topics.definition: BETWEEN checks whether a value lies between two endpoints, including both endpoints.
bullets: value BETWEEN low AND high includes low and high.
The module’s officeCode BETWEEN 1 AND 3 includes 1, 2, and 3.
A NULL comparison does not become TRUE merely because it uses BETWEEN.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The BETWEEN operator returns TRUE if a value is in a range of values

example.text:
SELECT firstName, lastName, officeCode
FROM employees
WHERE officeCode BETWEEN 1 AND 3
ORDER BY officeCode;

topics.title: LIKE — Match a Text Pattern
topics.definition: LIKE tests text against a pattern.
bullets: Use % for zero or more characters.
Use _ for exactly one character.
A pattern such as %son matches text ending in son.
Case matching depends on the string’s collation.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The LIKE operator evaluates to TRUE if a value matches a specified pattern.

example.text:
SELECT firstName, lastName
FROM employees
WHERE lastName LIKE '%son'
ORDER BY firstName;

topics.title: Percent and Underscore Wildcards
topics.definition: LIKE patterns use % and _ to describe variable parts of text.
bullets: % can match an empty string or several characters.
_ matches exactly one character.
These symbols are pattern wildcards inside LIKE, not universal replacements in every SQL expression.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
The % wildcard matches any string of zero or more 
characters while the _ wildcard matches any single character

rows: A followed by exactly one character

topics.title: AND — All Conditions Must Be True
topics.definition: AND returns TRUE only when every operand is TRUE.
bullets: Any FALSE operand makes the result FALSE.
If no operand is FALSE but one is UNKNOWN, the result is UNKNOWN.
It is used in WHERE and join conditions.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The AND operator is a logical operator that combines two or more Boolean

topics.title: AND with NULL — Truth Table
topics.definition: AND follows three-valued logic when NULL represents an unknown condition.
bullets: FALSE AND NULL is FALSE.
TRUE AND NULL is NULL; NULL AND NULL is NULL.
In MySQL/MariaDB Boolean expressions, 1 represents TRUE and 0 represents FALSE.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The following table illustrates the results of the AND operator

topics.title: AND Short-Circuit Evaluation
topics.definition: AND can stop evaluating once a FALSE operand determines the result.
bullets: The module’s 1 = 0 AND 1 / 0 returns 0.
The second expression need not be evaluated after the first is false.
Short-circuiting is an evaluation behavior, not a reason to write unsafe calculations.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: This function is called short-circuit evaluation

example.text: SELECT 1 = 0 AND 1 / 0;

topics.title: More Than Two AND Conditions
topics.definition: AND can require several filters at the same time.
bullets: Every condition must be true for a row to qualify.
The module combines USA, California, and a credit limit greater than 100000.
The > operator excludes the boundary itself; > 100000 does not include 100000.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: combine more than two Boolean expressions.

example.text:
SELECT customerName, country, state, creditLimit
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'USA'
  AND state = 'CA'
  AND creditLimit > 100000;

topics.title: OR — At Least One Condition Must Be True
topics.definition: OR returns TRUE when either or both operands are TRUE.
bullets: FALSE OR FALSE is FALSE.
TRUE OR TRUE is also TRUE; OR is inclusive.
Use it when a row may satisfy alternative conditions.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
returns true when 
either condition is true

corrections.text: Page 78 says only one expression is true. SQL OR also returns TRUE when both conditions are true.
corrections.label: MariaDB logical OR

topics.title: OR with NULL — Truth Table
topics.definition: OR with an unknown operand is TRUE if the other operand is TRUE; otherwise it remains unknown.
bullets: TRUE OR NULL is TRUE.
FALSE OR NULL is NULL; NULL OR NULL is NULL.
WHERE keeps only TRUE, so an unknown result does not select a row.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The following table shows the result of the OR operator.

topics.title: OR Short-Circuit Evaluation
topics.definition: OR can stop evaluating once a TRUE operand determines the result.
bullets: The module’s 1 = 1 OR 1 / 0 returns 1.
The division expression need not be evaluated after the first operand is true.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: MySQL uses short-circuit evaluation for the OR operator.

example.text: SELECT 1 = 1 OR 1 / 0;

corrections.text: Page 84 implies a SELECT division by zero necessarily throws an error. MariaDB SELECT division by zero returns NULL, with a warning depending on SQL mode. Strict INSERT/UPDATE can fail.
corrections.label: MariaDB division operator

topics.title: Operator Precedence — AND Before OR
topics.definition: AND has higher precedence than OR in MySQL/MariaDB.
bullets: TRUE OR FALSE AND FALSE means TRUE OR (FALSE AND FALSE).
The module’s example returns TRUE, displayed as 1.
Write parentheses when the default grouping is not your intention.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
MySQL always 
evaluates the OR operators after the AND operators.

example.text: SELECT TRUE OR FALSE AND FALSE;

topics.title: Parentheses — Control Logical Grouping
topics.definition: Parentheses group conditions so the query applies them together.
bullets: (USA OR France) AND creditLimit > 100000 applies the limit to both countries.
Without those parentheses, AND applies first and the USA branch can bypass the limit.
Parentheses clarify meaning even when the default precedence would produce the same result.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: WHERE (country = 'USA'

example.text:
SELECT customerName, country, creditLimit
FROM customers
WHERE (country = 'USA' OR country = 'France')
  AND creditLimit > 100000;

topics.title: SQL Join
topics.definition: A join combines rows from different tables using a matching rule.
bullets: It lets a result include columns stored in separate tables.
A join condition determines how rows relate.
Tables need not have a declared foreign key to be joined, although foreign keys often describe the relationship.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: A SQL Join is used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a

rows: All left rows plus their matches
All right rows plus their matches

topics.title: INNER JOIN — Matching Rows
topics.definition: INNER JOIN returns combinations whose join condition evaluates to TRUE.
bullets: Unmatched rows are excluded.
If nothing matches, the result is empty.
A source row with several matches appears in several result rows.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The INNER JOIN matches each row in one table with every row in other tables

topics.title: ON and Join Condition
topics.definition: ON introduces the condition that decides which row pairs match.
bullets: A typical condition compares related key values using =.
Qualify repeated column names with their table names or aliases.
Only a TRUE condition creates an INNER JOIN match.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The join condition specifies the rule for matching rows

example.text:
SELECT p.productCode, pl.textDescription
FROM products AS p
INNER JOIN productlines AS pl
  ON p.productLine = pl.productLine;

topics.title: AS — Column and Table Aliases
topics.definition: AS assigns a temporary name for a column or table inside a query.
bullets: m is the short name for members in FROM members AS m.
m.name identifies the name column from that table.
name AS member changes the output label, not the stored column name.
Table aliases can also be written without AS.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
FROM 
members as m

example.text:
SELECT m.name AS member
FROM members AS m;

topics.title: USING — Equal Same-Named Join Columns
topics.definition: USING matches equal values in a named column present in both joined tables.
bullets: USING (productLine) is a shorter equality join on the shared column name.
Use ON when names differ or a more complex condition is needed.
A NULL value does not equal another NULL in a normal equality join.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: you can use the USING clause

topics.title: Joining More Than Two Tables
topics.definition: A query can chain several joins, each with its own matching rule.
bullets: Start with a table in FROM, then add the related tables.
Each join uses the result built so far.
An INNER JOIN at any stage can remove combinations that have no match.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: INNER JOIN t2 ON join_condition1

example.text:
SELECT o.orderNumber, od.productCode, p.productName
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN orderdetails AS od ON od.orderNumber = o.orderNumber
INNER JOIN products AS p ON p.productCode = od.productCode;

topics.title: Products and Product Lines — Foreign Key Link
topics.definition: products.productLine refers to the product line recorded in productlines.
bullets: The productLine values connect product rows to their line description.
Join them to retrieve productCode, productName, and textDescription together.
The foreign key is the referring column in products.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
column productLine in the table 
products is called the foreign key column

topics.title: Order Details — Composite Primary Key
topics.definition: The orderdetails diagram identifies one composite primary key containing orderNumber and productCode.
bullets: The pair identifies an order line in the module’s model.
orderNumber also connects each line to its order.
A composite primary key is one key with multiple columns, not two separate primary keys.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
See the following orders and 
orderdetails tables:
sourceEvidence.visual: orders/orderdetails diagram: asterisks mark orderNumber and productCode in orderdetails

topics.title: GROUP BY — Summarize Joined Rows
topics.definition: GROUP BY gathers rows with the same grouping values for aggregate calculations.
bullets: Join orders to orderdetails to access each order’s lines.
SUM(quantityOrdered * priceEach) calculates a constructed line-total sum per order.
Group the selected order number and status when producing one result per order.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: using the INNER JOIN clause with the GROUP BY clause:

example.text:
SELECT o.orderNumber, o.status,
       SUM(od.quantityOrdered * od.priceEach) AS totalSales
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN orderdetails AS od ON od.orderNumber = o.orderNumber
GROUP BY o.orderNumber, o.status;

corrections.text: Page 93 describes total sales and shows a result but omits the query. This example is constructed from the diagram, not quoted from the PDF.
corrections.label: MariaDB GROUP BY

topics.title: FULL OUTER JOIN — Dialect Note
topics.definition: The FULL OUTER JOIN concept preserves unmatched rows from both sides as well as matches.
bullets: The module mentions this concept in its objectives and summary.
MySQL/MariaDB do not provide native FULL OUTER JOIN syntax.
Do not treat a FULL JOIN statement from another dialect as directly executable MySQL syntax.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: full outer joins.

corrections.text: The module describes FULL OUTER JOIN under MySQL. It is a valid SQL concept, but native MySQL/MariaDB JOIN syntax does not include it.
corrections.label: MariaDB JOIN syntax

topics.title: LEFT JOIN — Keep Every Left Row
topics.definition: LEFT JOIN retains every row from the table on its left, with matching right rows when available.
bullets: The table before LEFT JOIN is the left table.
Unmatched left rows receive NULL in right-table columns.
Several right-side matches can produce several result rows for one left row.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: the left join selects all data from the left table

topics.title: LEFT JOIN — Find Unmatched Rows
topics.definition: A LEFT JOIN followed by an IS NULL test can find left rows with no right-side match.
bullets: Test a right-side key that cannot be NULL in a real matched row.
The module uses c.committee_id IS NULL to find members without a matching committee row.
IS NULL tests missing values; = NULL does not perform this test.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
find rows in the left table that does not have 
corresponding rows in the right table.

example.text:
SELECT m.member_id, m.name
FROM members AS m
LEFT JOIN committees AS c USING (name)
WHERE c.committee_id IS NULL;

topics.title: Customers and Orders — One-to-Many Relationship
topics.definition: One customer can have zero or more orders; each order belongs to one customer in the module’s model.
bullets: customers.customerNumber identifies the customer.
orders.customerNumber links an order to that customer.
An all-customers LEFT JOIN keeps customers even when they have no orders.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: Each customer can have zero or more orders while each order must belong to one

topics.title: Customers Without Orders
topics.definition: Filter the joined order key for NULL to find customers who have no matching order.
bullets: LEFT JOIN retains all customers before the filter.
A missing order produces NULL in orderNumber and status.
USING (customerNumber) is available when both join columns share that name.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: find customers who have no order:

example.text:
SELECT c.customerNumber, c.customerName
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customerNumber = c.customerNumber
WHERE o.orderNumber IS NULL;

topics.title: RIGHT JOIN — Keep Every Right Row
topics.definition: RIGHT JOIN retains every row from the table on its right, with matching left rows when available.
bullets: The table after RIGHT JOIN is the right table.
Unmatched right rows receive NULL in left-table columns.
RIGHT OUTER JOIN is another spelling of RIGHT JOIN.
USING is available for equality joins on same-named columns.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: the column of the left table will have NULL in the final result set

corrections.text: Page 101 reverses the missing side. An unmatched RIGHT JOIN row keeps the right-table values; the left-table columns become NULL. Page 100 explains this correctly.
corrections.label: MariaDB JOIN syntax

topics.title: Customers and Sales Representatives — Optional Reference
topics.definition: customers.salesRepEmployeeNumber links a customer to employees.employeeNumber.
bullets: One employee can be responsible for zero or more customers.
A customer has zero or one assigned sales representative in the module’s model.
NULL salesRepEmployeeNumber means that customer has no assigned representative.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: salesRepEmployeeNumber in the table customers links to the column

topics.title: All Employees and Their Customers
topics.definition: Put employees on the right of a RIGHT JOIN to keep employees with no customer match.
bullets: Matching customers are displayed alongside their employee.
An employee without customers has NULL in the customer-side columns.
ORDER BY employeeNumber controls the result order.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: RIGHT JOIN returns all rows from the table employees

example.text:
SELECT e.employeeNumber, c.customerNumber
FROM customers AS c
RIGHT JOIN employees AS e
  ON c.salesRepEmployeeNumber = e.employeeNumber
ORDER BY e.employeeNumber;

topics.title: RIGHT JOIN — Find Unmatched Rows
topics.definition: A RIGHT JOIN followed by an IS NULL test can find right rows with no left-side match.
bullets: The module uses customerNumber IS NULL to find employees responsible for no customers.
Test a left-side non-nullable key so a genuine matched row cannot be mistaken for a missing match.
Reversing the table order allows the same preservation pattern to be expressed with LEFT JOIN.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: WHERE customerNumber is NULL

example.text:
SELECT e.employeeNumber
FROM customers AS c
RIGHT JOIN employees AS e
  ON c.salesRepEmployeeNumber = e.employeeNumber
WHERE c.customerNumber IS NULL
ORDER BY e.employeeNumber;
